title: Sangeeta Kujur vs Vijay Kujur Son Of Fedrick Kujur on 1 November, 2022

paragraphs.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF JHARKHAND AT RANCHI
 (Civil Appellate Jurisdiction)

 FA No. 409 of 2018
 -----
Sangeeta Kujur, wife of Mr. Vijay Kujur, daughter of Flora Lakra, resident of
Tiril Road, Kokar, Bariatu, PO & PS Bariatu, District Ranchi at present
residing at Office of French Embassy, 68-Sundar Nagar, PS Nizamuddin PO
Zorbagh, New Delhi-110003. ... .... Appellant
 Versus
Vijay Kujur son of Fedrick Kujur, resident of village Kokar, Tiril, PO & PS
Bariatu, District-Ranchi ... .... Respondent
 -------
CORAM : HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHREE CHANDRASHEKHAR
 HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE RATNAKER BHENGRA
 ------
 For the Appellant(s) : Mr. Satish Kumar Keshri, Advocate
 Mr.Neel Kamal, Advocate
 For the Respondent : Mr. Shyam Narsaria, Advocate
 ------
 ORDER

1st November 2022
Per, Shree Chandrashekhar,J.

We have examined the additional documents sought to be produced
by the appellant as additional documents. However, keeping in mind the principles
under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure , we do not find it
necessary to take these documents on record as additional documents because
these documents are completely unrelated to the issue arising in this case and are
not necessary to pronounce judgment in the present case.
2. IA No. 9845 of 2022 stands disposed of.

3. Sangeeta Kujur filed a petition under section 10(1)(x) of the Divorce
Act, 1869 seeking dissolution of her marriage solemnized with Vijay Kujur on
22nd April 2007. This petition was registered as Original Suit No. 473 of 2016 (in
short, "divorce suit") which has been dismissed on contest by the judgment dated
30th July 2018.

4. This First Appeal has been preferred by the wife on the ground that
the Family Court has misconstrued meaning of the expression 'cruelty' as envisaged
under section 10(1)(x) of the Divorce Act, 1869, inasmuch as, false accusations on
her character by the respondent would amount to mental cruelty which shall be a
ground for divorce.

5. For examining the aforesaid plea, it is necessary to have a glance
 2 FA No. 409 of 2018




through discussions by the Family Court in the divorce suit, which are as follows:

"9. From the fact mentioned in the present suit, it appears that
 petitioner Sangeeta Kujur is presently residing at Delhi. According
 to case of petitioner marriage between the parties was solemnized
 on 22.04.2007 as per Christian (Catholic) rituals at Kokar Ranchi.
 In the petition allegation about the alleged cruelty and bad habits
 of respondent is made but in the evidence of petitioner herself (the
 only witness examined on her behalf), these allegations and facts
 stated in petition have not been stated to corroborate and support
 these facts. The only witness examined on behalf of petitioner is
 Sangeeta Kujur, the petitioner herself. In her examination-in-chief
 which is an affidavited statement running in seven paragraphs no
 where any specific instance of cruelty is mentioned. One Xerox
 Copy of Police intimation has been brought on the record and same
 is marked exhibit 'X'. This exhibit marked 'X' for identification is a
 letter addressed to S.H.O., Nizammaldin Police Station Delhi,
 wherein it is stated that a complaint is being made by petitioner
 against her husband. It is mentioned that husband used to do
 beating and therefore the complainant (wife) does not want to live
 with him. This letter to SHO appears a vague cryptic information
 not mentioning date, time and place of alleged beating incident and
 it appears that because of this ambiguity even no formal FIR has
 been registered and any action taken by the concerned Police.
 Apart from this there is nothing on record which may show any
 alleged cruelty on the part of respondent in the present case. If one
 goes through the examination-in-chief filed on affidavit under
 Order-XVIII Rule-4 (1) CPC no material facts regarding the
 allegations of any cruelty are stated by the petitioner. There is
 reference of an information given to Kokar Police, Ranchi about
 alleged threat given by the respondent, but said FIR is not brought
 on the record.

10. On behalf of the respondent/wife two witnesses have been
 examined. The respondent witness no. I is Vijay Kujur, the
 respondent himself, in his examination-in-chief he has stated that
 the petitioner has developed intimacy with one Ankit who was
 tenant in the house and upon objection she started quarreling with
 him. Even both of them have beaten the respondent. He has denied
 the allegation of cruelty as alleged in the petition of Sangeeta
 Kujur. Another witness Jems Nayan Toppo has also stated that
 petitioner Sangeeta Kujur has developed intimacy with Ankit even
 she used to give him money.

11. From the appreciation of evidence available on the record, 1
 do find that the facts alleged in the petition by petitioner-wife
 Sangeeta Kujur are not found proved and established in her
 evidence and therefore I am of the view that petitioner has failed to
 establish her case making a ground of divorce by dissolution of
 marriage. Accordingly issue no.-III is decided against the
 petitioner."

6. Mr. Satish Kumar Keshri, the learned counsel for the appellant has
urged that in her evidence the appellant referred to the divorce petition and while
so the allegations made by her in the petition for divorce can be read into the
evidence. The learned counsel for the appellant would submit that the complaint
filed by the appellant a copy of which was marked as Ext-X (for identification), if
read in the background of the allegations made by the appellant in the divorce suit,
would amount to mental cruelty as explained by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
 3 FA No. 409 of 2018




" Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh " (2007) 4 SCC 511.

7. The learned counsel for the appellant has also relied on the following
judgments:

( i) "Smt. Kakali Das v. Dr. Asish Kumar Das "AIR 2004 Calcutta
176; ( ii)"Joydeep Majumdar v. Bharti Jaiswal Majumdar" LL 2021 SC 117, and;
( iii) "Meenu Devi v. Amit Kumar " 2018 (3) JLJR 468.

8. The expression 'cruelty' as can be gathered from the language
employed under section 10(1)(x) of the Divorce Act, 1869 would mean that if the
petitioner has been treated by the other spouse in such manner as to cause a
reasonable apprehension in the mind of the petitioner that it would be harmful and
injurious to live with the respondent, such acts of the other spouse would amount to
cruelty so as to make the petitioner entitled for a decree of divorce.
9. Section 10(1)(x) of the Divorce Act, 1869 provides as under:

"10. Grounds for dissolution of marriage.--(1) Any marriage
 solemnized, whether before or after the commencement of the
 Indian Divorce (Amendment) Act, 2001, may, on a petition
 presented to the District Court either by the husband or the wife, be
 dissolved on the ground that since the solemnization of the
 marriage, the respondent--

(x) has treated the petitioner with such cruelty as to cause a
 reasonable apprehension in the mind of the petitioner that it would
 be harmful or injurious for the petitioner to live with the
 respondent."

10. In " Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh " (2007) 4 SCC 511, on which the
learned counsel for the appellant has placed heavy reliance, the Hon'ble Supreme
Court has observed as under:

"101. No uniform standard can ever be laid down for guidance, yet
 we deem it appropriate to enumerate some instances of human
 behaviour which may be relevant in dealing with the cases of
 "mental cruelty". The instances indicated in the succeeding
 paragraphs are only illustrative and not exhaustive:

(i) On consideration of complete matrimonial life of the parties,
 acute mental pain, agony and suffering as would not make possible
 for the parties to live with each other could come within the broad
 parameters of mental cruelty.

(ii) On comprehensive appraisal of the entire matrimonial life of
 the parties, it becomes abundantly clear that situation is such that
 the wronged party cannot reasonably be asked to put up with such
 conduct and continue to live with other party.

(iii) Mere coldness or lack of affection cannot amount to cruelty,
 frequent rudeness of language, petulance of manner, indifference
 and neglect may reach such a degree that it makes the married life
 for the other spouse absolutely intolerable.

(iv) Mental cruelty is a state of mind. The feeling of deep anguish,
 disappointment, frustration in one spouse caused by the conduct of
 other for a long time may lead to mental cruelty.

(v) A sustained course of abusive and humiliating treatment
 calculated to torture, discommode or render miserable life of the
 spouse.

(vi) Sustained unjustifiable conduct and behaviour of one spouse
 actually affecting physical and mental health of the other spouse.

The treatment complained of and the resultant danger or
 apprehension must be very grave, substantial and weighty.

(vii) Sustained reprehensible conduct, studied neglect, indifference
 or total departure from the normal standard of conjugal kindness
 causing injury to mental health or deriving sadistic pleasure can
 also amount to mental cruelty.

(viii) The conduct must be much more than jealousy, selfishness,
 possessiveness, which causes unhappiness and dissatisfaction and
 emotional upset may not be a ground for grant of divorce on the
 ground of mental cruelty.

(ix) Mere trivial irritations, quarrels, normal wear and tear of the
 married life which happens in day-to-day life would not be
 adequate for grant of divorce on the ground of mental cruelty.

(x) The married life should be reviewed as a whole and a few
 isolated instances over a period of years will not amount to cruelty.
 The ill conduct must be persistent for a fairly lengthy period, where
 the relationship has deteriorated to an extent that because of the
 acts and behaviour of a spouse, the wronged party finds it
 extremely difficult to live with the other party any longer, may
 amount to mental cruelty.

(xi) If a husband submits himself for an operation of sterilisation
 without medical reasons and without the consent or knowledge of
 his wife and similarly, if the wife undergoes vasectomy or abortion
 without medical reason or without the consent or knowledge of her
 husband, such an act of the spouse may lead to mental cruelty.

(xii) Unilateral decision of refusal to have intercourse for
 considerable period without there being any physical incapacity or
 valid reason may amount to mental cruelty.

(xiii) Unilateral decision of either husband or wife after marriage
 not to have child from the marriage may amount to cruelty.

(xiv) Where there has been a long period of continuous separation,
 it may fairly be concluded that the matrimonial bond is beyond
 repair. The marriage becomes a fiction though supported by a legal
 tie. By refusing to sever that tie, the law in such cases, does not
 serve the sanctity of marriage; on the contrary, it shows scant
 regard for the feelings and emotions of the parties. In such like
 situations, it may lead to mental cruelty."

11. In the backdrop of the judgment in "Samar Ghosh", if evidence of
the appellant is read, it can be seen that there is no specific instance of any act or
omission on part of the respondent which can be construed to mean and fall under
the expression 'cruelty'.

12. For the sake of clarity, we would extract whole of the examination-in-
chief of the appellant which contains only eight sentences running across seven
paragraphs.
13. In her examination-in-chief, the appellant has stated as under:

"I, Sangeeta Kujur, D/o Flora Lakra, R/o TIRIL Road Kokar, P.O.
 & P.S. Bariatu, Dist. Ranchi PIN 834009, states as
 follows:-

1. That the above mentioned case is filed U/s. (10) (i) (x) of the
 Divorce Amendment Act, 2001.
2. That the case is under Heading of Evidence.

3. That the petitioner submits the case issue has been
 5 FA No. 409 of 2018




 settled as Cruelty & Desertion (Main ground).

4. That earlier in September 2016 petitioner filed under
 affidavit revealing Desertion since three years between the parties.

5. That at the time of filing Original Application
 petitioner filed proof of Cruelty by way of Documentary Evidence.
 Exhibit - 1 marked-X(for identification).

6. That petitioner prays the Documentary Evidence be
 exhibited for the convenience of the Court & parties.

7. It is pertinent to note that petitioner on 21 st Dec.2017
 appeared in the Hon'ble Family Court and returned back to Delhi
 by evening Flight in between opposite party Vijay Kujur and his
 brother reached the parental house and threatened dire
 consequences. On 22nd Dec. petitioner again came to Ranchi by
 Flight and reported the complain in Police Station (Sadar) Kokar,
 Ranchi."

14. The marriage between the parties was solemnized according to
Christian (Catholic) rituals and practices on 22 nd April 2007 and out of their
wedlock two children were born. The appellant is employed with French Embassy
and posted at New Delhi where, according to the respondent, she developed
relationship with Ankit Yadav who is a tenant in their house. In her petition for
divorce, the appellant made allegations that the respondent has bad drinking habit
and of consuming tobacco which in spite of her insistence the respondent did not
give up. But in her evidence in the Court, the appellant has not stated even these
facts. The appellant has admitted in the cross-examination that her marriage with
the respondent was a love marriage. But in her evidence, except referring to a
complaint made with the police in which she has alleged that the respondent abused
and assaulted her, she has said nothing at all about cruelty inflicted upon her by the
respondent. This is consistent case of the respondent that on account of intimacy
with Ankit Yadav his wife refused to discharge her matrimonial obligations and
was, in fact, living with the said Ankit Yadav in live-in relationship. On the
contrary, the appellant filed an information with Nizammuddin Police at New Delhi
but the said complaint was not even converted into a First Information Report.

15. In the first place, such complaint/information is of no consequence
inasmuch as the appellant has not said a word about mental agony and harassment
suffered by her on account of acts of her husband for which she filed complaint
with the police. As noticed hereinabove, the appellant has failed to tender any
evidence much less evidence of such nature which could have probabilized her case
that the respondent has been inflicting mental cruelty upon her. Even if the
information by the appellant to the police is taken into account, the appellant has
failed to demonstrate how she has suffered loss of reputation or any injury on
account of the acts of her husband - her evidence is completely silent on this
aspect. In the cross-examination, the appellant has stated that the main reason for
 6 FA No. 409 of 2018




quarrel between the couple was that the respondent was suspecting her chastity. In
the cross-examination, specific suggestions as regards her intimacy with Ankit
Yadav were put to her which, of course, she has denied. But, at the same time, she
has also stated that she does not want any reconciliation with her husband. She has
further stated that she is staying away from the company of her husband for the last
three years. In " Joydeep Majumdar v. Bharti Jaiswal Majumdar" LL 2021 SC 117
the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed that normal wear and tear of the middle
class married life shall not be construed as a broken marital relationship.

16. The plea urged on behalf of the appellant that the allegations made in
the petition for divorce may be considered to have been incorporated in her
examination-in-chief cannot be accepted. If this course of procedure is adopted that
would definitely cause injustice to the respondent and would be in breach of the
rules of natural justice as the respondent had no opportunity to answer the case of
the appellant, as sought to have been projected before this Court. By the Act 22 of
2002, Rule 4 to Order XVIII has been amended in the Code of Civil Procedure to
provide a speedy mechanism for disposal of suits under which the parties are
permitted to file their examination-in-chief on affidavit. A statement which does not
form part of the examination-in-chief of the appellant cannot be read as her
evidence. The reason is that the pleadings are no substitute for proof and also
because such statements in the pleadings are not available to have been subjected to
cross-examination.

17. This is fundamental in law that the allegations in the pleadings of the
parties shall not be treated as evidence. Order VI Rule 1 of the Code of Civil
Procedure provides that pleadings shall mean plaint and written statement. The
provisions under Order VI contain a bar under Rule 2 to the effect that every
pleadings shall contain; with further emphasis on "and contain only", statements in
a concise form of the material facts but not the evidence by which they are to be
proved. No doubt, Rule 2 has a reference to the evidence that the parties may lay in
course of trial but this much is clear from the said rule that pleadings and evidence
are two different things which are laid at two different stages in the civil
proceedings.

18. In " Manager, Reserve Bank of India, Bangalore v. S. Mani & Ors. "
(2005) 5 SCC 100 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under:

"19. Pleadings are no substitute for proof. No workman, thus, took
 an oath to state that they had worked for 240 days. No document
 in support of the said plea was produced. It is, therefore not
 correct to contend that the plea raised by the respondents herein
 that they had worked continuously for 240 days was deemed to
 have been admitted by applying the doctrine of non-traverse. In
 any event the contention of the respondents having been denied
 7 FA No. 409 of 2018




 and disputed, it was obligatory on the part of the respondents to
 add new evidence. The contents raised in the letters of the union
 dated 30-5-1988 and 11-4-1990 containing statements to the effect
 that the workmen had been working continuously for 240 days
 might not have been replied to, but the same is of no effect as by
 reason thereof, the allegations made therein cannot be said to have
 been proved, particularly in view of the fact that the contents
 thereof were not proved by any witness. Only by reason of non-
 response to such letters, the contents thereof would not stand
 admitted. The Evidence Act does not say so."

19. In yet another case, in " Ayaaubkhan Noorkhan Pathan v. State of
Maharashtra " (2013) 4 SCC 465 the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed that an
affidavit is not "evidence" within the meaning of Section 3 of the Evidence Act,
1872.
20. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as under:

"31. It is a settled legal proposition that an affidavit is not
 "evidence" within the meaning of Section 3 of the Evidence Act,
 1872 (hereinafter referred to as "the Evidence Act "). Affidavits are,
 therefore, not included within the purview of the definition of
 "evidence" as has been given in Section 3 of the Evidence Act, and
 the same can be used as "evidence" only if, for sufficient reasons,
 the court passes an order under Order 19 of the Code of Civil
 Procedure , 1908 (hereinafter referred to as " CPC "). Thus, the
 filing of an affidavit of one's own statement, in one's own favour,
 cannot be regarded as sufficient evidence for any court or tribunal,
 on the basis of which it can come to a conclusion as regards a
 particular fact situation. ( Vide Sudha Devi v. M.P. Narayanan and
 Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani )"

21. The learned counsel for the appellant has referred to paragraph no.28
of the cross-examination of the respondent who tendered evidence as RW1, to
indicate that the respondent has admitted that he did not see illicit relationship of
the appellant with Ankit Yadav. This statement of the respondent has been referred
to by the learned counsel for the appellant to submit that the respondent has been
making false allegation of adultery against the appellant. To fortify this submission,
the learned counsel for the appellant has referred to the judgment in "Joydeep
Majumdar" to submit that baseless complaints which cause harm to the reputation
of a person shall also come within the meaning of mental cruelty.
22. Paragraph No. 28 of the cross-examination of RW1 reads as under:

"28. eSa vius vkWa[kksa ls vkosnhdk vkSj vafdr dk uktk;t lEca/k gksrs ugha ns[kkA
 vkosnhdk dk Qksu esa vkosnhdk vkSj vafdr dk QksVk eSlst] pSfVax ns[ksAa "
English Translation:

"28. I have not seen the applicant and Ankit engaged in illicit
 relationship. I have seen photo-message and chatting of the applicant
 and Ankit in the phone of the applicant."

23. In the context of admission of the respondent in paragraph No.28 of
the cross-examination, we would only indicate that whole of the said paragraph has
 8 FA No. 409 of 2018




to be read together. Not only that, the evidence of the respondent has to be read
together and not in piecemeal. The statement of the respondent that he has not seen
the appellant engaged in sexual intercourse with Ankit Yadav cannot be read in
isolation. The respondent has said that he found evidence of relationship of the
appellant with Ankit Yadav in their photo-messages and chatting in the mobile
phone of the appellant. Moreover, evidence of the respondent in a matrimonial
petition cannot be the basis to grant relief to the petitioner.

24. In " State of M.P. v. Nomi Singh " (2015) 14 SCC 450 the Hon'ble
Supreme Court has observed as under:

"11. It is settled principle of law that in respect of relief claimed by
 a plaintiff, he has to stand on his own legs by proving his case...."

25. In view of the aforesaid discussions, we do not find any reason to
interfere with the judgment dated 30th July 2018 passed in Original Suit No. 473 of
2016 and, accordingly, this First Appeal is dismissed.

(Shree Chandrashekhar, J.)


 (Ratnaker Bhengra, J.)
Jharkhand High Court, Ranchi
Dated: 1st November, 2022
SB/Nibha-AFR
